subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Power of Naming
description: One-minute skill: The Power of Naming.

hook.text: Russian speakers have separate words for light blue and dark blue. They literally see those blues as more different.

buildup.text: Lera Boroditsky tested it: Russian speakers distinguished blue shades faster when the colors crossed their linguistic boundary.

discovery.text: Having a name for something sharpens perception. Labels carve continuous spectra into discrete categories.

twist.text: The effect disappears when you give the speakers a verbal distraction task. Language is doing the heavy lifting.

climax.text: Wine experts taste better partly because they have more words. Names don't just describe experience—they shape it.

punchline.text: Name it and you see it differently.

quiz.question: How do extra color words affect perception?

details.summary: Naming things changes how we perceive and remember them. Learning a label for a color makes it easier to discriminate. Categorizing an emotion with a word helps regulate it.
details.whyItMatters: Naming is not passive labeling; it actively shapes perception and cognition. The words available to us influence what we see, feel, and remember.
takeaways: Labels sharpen perceptual distinctions between categories
Naming emotions helps regulate them (affect labeling)
Verbal labels influence attention, memory, and categorization

faq.question: How does naming an emotion help regulate it?
faq.answer: Brain imaging shows that labeling a negative emotion reduces amygdala activation. The process of putting a feeling into words engages prefrontal regulation circuits. This is called affect labeling or feelings into words.

faq.question: Can naming ever hurt cognition?
faq.answer: Yes. Verbal overshadowing occurs when describing a face in words impairs later visual recognition. The verbal description overwrites the richer visual memory. In wine tasting, verbalizing flavor profiles can distort perception.
